analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from letting AI systems make or drive hiring, firing, and work-condition decisions without human oversight, testing, disclosure, and appeal rights.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 4 cosponsors in July 2023, the bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill says employers with 11 or more workers cannot let a software system be the sole decision-maker in hiring, firing, discipline, pay, scheduling, or promotion. Before using AI output in any of those decisions, employers would have to test it for discrimination, audit it yearly, tell workers how it works, have a human corroborate the result, give the worker a plain-language explanation within 7 days, and let the worker dispute it and appeal to a different human. Workers managed by an algorithm could opt out and get a human manager. The bill creates a new Labor Department division to enforce it, protects workers who complain, and lets workers and unions sue for damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants and workers at covered employers — including gig and contract workers — who would gain the right to know when an algorithm is judging them, see the reasoning, contest the outcome to a person, and appeal to another person. Workers who are discriminated against by biased systems, penalized by automated productivity scoring, or managed entirely by an app would get damages of $5,000–$40,000 per violation and a path to court that arbitration agreements cannot block. Unions could also sue.

how_it_helps.text: Employers may not rely exclusively on an automated decision system for any hiring, firing, discipline, pay, scheduling, or promotion decision [S2].

Before using AI output, employers must pre-test it for discriminatory impact against race, sex, age, disability, and other protected traits, and must have it independently re-tested for bias every year with results made public [S2].

Workers must be told, before a decision, that an automated system is being used, what data feeds it, and how to dispute it — and within 7 days of any decision they must get a plain-language explanation and a machine-readable copy of their input data [S2].
Every AI-informed decision must be corroborated by a human with relevant experience, and the worker may appeal to a different human [S2].
Workers managed through an automated system can opt out and be managed by a human instead [S2].

Workers and unions can sue for actual or statutory damages ($5,000–$20,000 per violation, up to $40,000 for willful or repeated ones), with attorney's fees, and predispute arbitration and class-action waivers cannot be enforced against these claims [S2].

The bill protects workers from retaliation for complaining or testifying about AI misuse, and creates a new Technology and Worker Protection Division in the Labor Department, plus state attorney general enforcement, to police it [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more workers — including public agencies — bear the costs of bias testing, annual independent audits, disclosure documents, human review of every AI-informed decision, appeals processes, and training. Companies selling AI hiring and workforce-management tools face a compliance and liability regime. Federal and state taxpayers fund the new Labor Department enforcement division. Some compliance cost could be passed to consumers or slow hiring processes.

drawbacks.text: The threshold is small — employers with just 11 workers are covered — so the testing, annual audits, disclosure, documentation, and appeal requirements would fall on many small businesses, not just large employers running sophisticated AI [S2].

The definition of an automated decision system is broad — any software that aids a decision through scores, metrics, or evaluations — so ordinary scheduling, applicant-tracking, or payroll tools could be swept in, multiplying paperwork for routine decisions [S2].

The bill creates a new federal division with appointed staff, four advisory boards, and a joint federal-state enforcement apparatus, a permanent expansion of the Labor Department's budget and reach [S2].

Requiring a human to corroborate every AI-informed decision and letting workers appeal each one could slow high-volume hiring and scheduling operations, and employers might respond by dropping useful tools rather than building compliant ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a real and growing problem — algorithmic hiring screens and productivity trackers that workers often cannot see or contest — and the core ideas (disclosure, bias testing, human appeal) are similar to rules several states and the EU have adopted. The honest cost is compliance burden: with a low 11-employee threshold and a sweeping definition of covered software, small employers using off-the-shelf tools would face real paperwork and legal exposure, and some may simply stop using decision-support tools. The design is ambitious rather than narrowly tailored, but the benefits to workers facing unreviewable automated decisions are substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in July 2023, and sat there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Casey introduced the bill on July 20, 2023, joined by Sens. Schatz, Fetterman, and Sanders as original cosponsors [S1].
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].

The action history shows no further steps: the committee never held a hearing or markup, the Senate never debated it, and no vote was ever held before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers using AI-driven hiring and management tools — and the vendors selling them — keep the status quo: no federal requirement for bias testing, disclosure, human review, or worker appeal rights. Workers subject to algorithmic decisions remain without a federal right to contest them.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the No Robot Bosses Act and gathered 4 cosponsors; the bill died in committee

for.name: Sens. Brian Schatz, John Fetterman, and Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; no further action recorded

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Bernie Sanders, I-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote during the two-year Congress

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator sponsored or cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the cross-party support typically needed to advance in the Senate

sides.party_line_note: All 5 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-led committee never moved it.

industries.industry: AI hiring and workforce-management software vendors
industries.note: Companies selling algorithmic hiring screens, productivity scorers, and scheduling systems would face mandatory bias testing, annual public audits, disclosure obligations, and statutory-damages liability up to $40,000 per worker per violation. Their interest in keeping deployment friction-free runs against workers' ability to see and contest the software's judgments.

industries.industry: Large employers using algorithmic management (warehousing, gig platforms, retail, staffing)
industries.note: Employers with 11 or more workers could no longer let software be the sole decision-maker and would need human corroboration, documentation, and appeals for AI-informed decisions on pay, scheduling, discipline, and firing. Firms that profit from automated discipline and productivity tracking would bear the cost of human oversight.

The bill's requirement for pre-deployment validation and annual independent bias testing — with results made public — would create a paid market for third-party algorithmic auditors. This industry's interest runs alongside workers', since its product is the testing that protects them.
